January 6th does tell us something about our country because it happened. We don't get to deny it. But here's the great thing. January 5th also happened and we've added aside which America was going to be. That's Senator and Reverend Raphael Warnock, the first black U.S. Senator from Georgia, elected just one day before the January 6th Capitol attack. I'm Margaret Hoover. This is the Firing Line Podcast. Senator Warnock's win a year and a half ago in a runoff election was not only historic. It helped the Democrats reclaim the Senate. God is up to something. Warnock has another calling. For the past 17 years, he's been a pastor at Atlanta's Ebenezer Baptist Church, a role once held by Martin Luther King Jr. Every now and then God gives us a glimpse of God's glory. I sat down with Senator Warnock on Capitol Hill to talk about his new memoir, The Big Issues, heading into the midterms, and his own closely watched re-election race. Republicans have nominated Herschel Walker, a football legend who has the backing of Trump to run against Warnock. You know, Herschel's not only a Georgia hero, he is an American legend. In recent years, Walker has courted plenty of controversy from lawsuits against his businesses to promoting conspiracy theories about the 2020 election. His claim about a COVID killing miss. As you walk through the door, it will cure any COVID on your body. has already made it into a Warnock campaign ad. Is Herschel Walker right for Georgia? Great thing about America is that's not up to me. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock, welcome to Firing Line. Great to be here. Thank you. You have a new book out, a way out of no way. And in it, you speak about two Americas. One America that historically voted for the first Black Senator from Georgia on January 5th, and another America that the very next day took part in a riot on the Capitol of the United States. As you watch the January 6th hearings, along with millions of Americans this week, which America is prevailing, Well, thank you so much. It's great to be here. First of all, let me say the title for the book, A Way Out of No Way, comes from the culture and tradition of the black church. And when we say the black church and let me hasten to say, we've never meant anything racially exclusive about that. We're talking about the anti-slavery church, the church that was literally born fighting for freedom. the conscience of the American churches pushing us towards this idea. As it says in scripture, one blood, God has made all nations to develop on the face of the earth. So it is that tradition that has animated my ministry that informs the work that I do. And eventually it got me to do something as crazy as run for the United States Senate. I enjoy being the pastor. And as you point out, Georgia did an amazing thing, a former state of the Confederacy, elected its first African-American senator, only the 11th African-American senator in the whole history of the country. It also elected its first Jewish senator in one fell swoop, and I think somewhere in glory, Martin Luther King Jr. and Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel. are smiling because they marched alongside one another. Rabbi Heschel said he felt like his feet were praying. And so I'm very proud of my state. I was born in Georgia, raised there, went to college there. And now I serve as pastor of Ebenezer Church, where Dr. King served. Georgia sent me and John Ossoff to the Senate on January 5th on the heels of a multiracial coalition. January 6th, we saw a violent assault on the Capitol. with signs that were anti-Semitic, racist, police were brutalized, people died, and all of it was driven by the big lie. This idea that certain people's votes and therefore their voices don't count in our democracy. And so for me, this is an America moment. January 6 does tell us something about our country because it happened. We don't get to deny it. But here's the great thing. January 5 also happens. and we've had to decide which America we're gonna be. Which side is prevailing right now? Oh, I think that that, look, I have a great faith in our country. And maybe it's because, you know, when I was born in 1969, Georgia was represented by two arch-segregationist senators. I now sit in the seat held by segregationists. And so I've seen not only in my life, but as I tell the story and my memoir, the life of my father and my mother, I've seen enough of the arc of American history to remain hopeful, to know that we can push closer to our ideals, but it takes hard work. My mom grew up in Waycross, Georgia in the 1950s. She used to pick somebody else's tobacco and cotton, but in the last election, she helped pick her youngest son. to be a United States Senator, only in America is my story possible. And that's why I get up every morning trying to fight for that American dream, the covenant we have with one another, E pluribus unum out of many one, a covenant big enough to embrace my two children and all of our children. You're from Georgia, a state that, as you well know, factored into President Trump's big lie and has come up in the January 6th hearings this week. It was the subject, of course, of the phone call that then President Trump made to Georgia's Secretary of State, Brad Raffensberger, when he asked him to, quote, help him find enough votes to overturn the election results. are the hearings helping to move this country forward? Again, I think January 6 tells us something about our country in this moment. Some truths are inconvenient and they're painful. And we don't get to pretend like it didn't happen. But January 5 also happened. And I think it's so important in this moment for all of us to stand up. This is not about any single person. The democracy doesn't belong to the politicians. And in a sense, I see January 6 as an extreme and radical expression of a problem that I see every day in our politics. And that is politics too often becomes about the politicians. It's about their power, who's up and who's down, who's in and who's out. And when you're focused on your own power, rather than the sanctity of the democracy itself. Then I think you're given, if not to violent assaults and expressions, but you're given to a kind of cynical politics that makes the politician their own biggest cause. So that when we encounter something that most Americans believe we ought to get some progress on, like common sense gun laws, It becomes very hard to do anything, even when nearly 90% of the country believes in it, because the politicians are thinking about themselves. And yet, this week, It was announced that there has a bipartisan framework arrived at that includes 10 Republican senators, Democratic senators, and the gun reform framework would include incentives for states to pass red flag laws, increased mental health resources, school safety money, enhancements to background checks for people under 21. Narrower, of course, than what many Democrats wanted and that what President Biden asked for. but it appears to have enough support to become a law. You have expressed, I've heard you over the course of the last couple of days, expressed support for the framework. If it becomes a bill, will you vote for it? Oh, I have great faith in Senator Chris Murphy and many of my colleagues were working on this. Here's what I said. After we witnessed this awful slaughter of children, of innocence, 19 babies killed in a school along with their teachers. What's really clear to me is that for the Senate to do nothing, that's clearly the wrong answer. And I was worried because we saw after Sandy Hook, no movement. And so we won't agree on everything that needs to be done. But we have to have movement. And so I was very much encouraged by the framework as it's been laid out. And I look forward to supporting a bill that'll make a difference and save some lives. So that's a yes. You're a yes vote. I support the framework as I've seen it. You voted last month on the Women's Health Protection Act. Absolutely. This is a bill you've talked about how you're a pro-choice preacher. And this is a bill that would codify the right of women to have an abortion. of the critics, including two Republican pro-choice senators, say that the bill went too far. It was too broad. They supported narrower version of the bill that would also codify the right for women to have an abortion. But their argument is that in their bill, it doesn't undercut the rights of health care providers who have religious objections to abortion. Are there circumstances under which you could support a bill like that drafted by Republicans who are pro-choice. I support a woman's right to choose, and I've been very clear about this. Look, I have a profound reverence for life. I also have a deep and abiding respect for choice. And I think that a patient's room is too narrow and cramped a space for a woman, her doctor, and the United States government. I just think that's too many people in the room. We should spend more time thinking about the things that we actually can work on. And often the public is closer. The American public is closer on these issues sometimes than what's reflected in our politics. So we've been at a kind of stalemate on this issue, at least in the politics for a long time. But I think about our maternal mortality rate in this country, which is abysmally high, especially in a state like Georgia. And black women are three to four times more likely to die in childbirth or as a result of labor than their white sisters, even when they have the income, even when they have the insurance, think about that. They're still dying at a much higher rate. And so I got together with Senator Marco Rubio. We don't agree on Roe, but he and I have put forward a maternal mortality bill that looks at this issue and tries to provide resources. It is unacceptable. of that black women are dying and that people in states like Georgia or that our maternal mortality rate is so high in this country as opposed to our other Western counterparts. We can do better than that. So I think if we can find the places where we can work together and not focus on the politicians but focus on the people, we can make progress. So do you think you would support or could support? Would you consider supporting? a bill that Republican pro-choice senators had put forward in order to codify rep. For me, it's not about Republican Democrat. It's not about- What about this distinction that it protects religious workers or people of religious conscience who don't have- I would need to see the text of the bill. I mean, that's part of what it means to be a good legislator. I take it very seriously. But I absolutely affirm a woman's right to choose. You know, I think the range of circumstances under which people find themselves is complicated in ways that doesn't fit in the narrow kind of politics that we see played out in Washington. In your book. a way out of no way, you're really clear actually about what you call the racist overtones that you see in quote Trump's claim that the election was stolen after black Americans voted in unprecedented numbers in 2020. You've worked and you write about this in your book on voting rights for many, many years, long before you got to the Senate. There have been several Senate votes on legislation for voting rights. Only one Republican by my count has voted for any one of those bills. That's Lisa Murkowski. But there's also been a door of a substantial Democratic support that can break the log jam and get over to 60. There's been missing Democratic votes and voting rights as well. So it occurs to me that seven Republicans voted to convict President Trump. And they might be a good starting point for refuting the big lie and creating new voting rights legislation. Do you think that there is a possibility the way gun control legislation has been at least a framework has been passed in a bipartisan way? The way you and Marco Rubio have worked on maternal mortality rates. Do you think there's a path for bipartisan voting reform? But voting rights used to be bipartisan. It ought to be bipartisan. The last time the voting rights law passed, the United States Senate, the vote was 96 to 0. And George W. Bush was the president of the United States. And so now we've seen a major shift. Some of the folks who voted for that bill are in the House or in the Senate right now. Look, there's nothing more precious, nothing more important than the right to vote. I often say that a vote is a kind of prayer for the kind of world we desire for ourselves and for our children. Democracy is for me, the political enactment of a spiritual idea. There's notion that all of us have within ourselves a spark of the divine, that we have value. And therefore, we ought to have a voice in the direction of the country and our destiny within it. This assault on voting rights flies in the face of what it means to be a country that is knit together on the basis of an idea, a democratic idea. And it's something that I've been fighting for long before I came to the United States Senate. We register voters at my church, because I think your voters, your voice, your voice is your human dignity, that spark of the divine. And not long after I came to Ebenezer Church, I discussed it a way out of no way, the way in which I came in 2005, right on the heels of Hurricane Katrina. And Ebenezer, like a lot of churches, was supporting the folks in New Orleans who had lost so much. A lot of those evacuees had been displaced to Atlanta. And that following spring, there was a municipal election. And very little to no preparations to help the folks who had been displaced to dozens of other states to get back home to vote. And many of them had to be there in person to vote. So our church organized something called the Freedom Caravan. And we took scores of Katrina evacuees back to New Orleans so that they could exercise their right to vote because I think it's that important. Here were folks who had lost everything and yet they wanted to go back to their own city and for their voices to be heard. And in this moment, it's so important that we get the people, their voices back in their democracy. You've worked with Stacey Abrams in Georgia and her new Georgia project to build a coalition that turned out Democrats in 2020. And she's back on the ballot this year in a rematch against Governor Brian Kemp. She says voter suppression is why she lost. And while we know she never fully conceded the race, a lot has happened since that election. And I wonder how you evaluate the efforts to engage more voters in Georgia and whether you think voter suppression will be as much of an issue in this upcoming election as she feels it wasn't her election. Well, we'll have to see how things turn out. But look, democracy is not a noun, it's a verb. we have to remain vigilant. And here's what I'm clear about. We have to make sure every eligible voter can cast their vote and that their voices are heard. When I talk about the issues that are confronting our democracy, I'm talking also about the outsized influence of dark money. in our politics. The voices of ordinary people have been squeezed out, replaced by dark money, partisan and racial gerrymandering. I believe in that American idea, one person, one vote, and we have to do everything we can to safeguard it. Has the work been done in Georgia to ensure that everyone who wants to vote will get to vote in the upcoming election? The work of democracy is ongoing, and we have to keep doing that work. I started out registering voters. And then I ended up running for office. And I didn't set out to do this. I'm a pastor and I enjoy being a pastor. I knew early on that I would pursue this route. But after having spent years fighting for Medicaid expansion, I came a few years ago to the Capitol, not as a senator, but as an activist. I was fighting for Medicaid expansion in 2014. And there was a bill that provided a huge tax cut to the top 1% in our country, tax cut to those who don't need it, about taking resources from those who need support. And so I and a group of ministers came to the Capitol and began to protest. They were taking resources away from the Children's Healthcare Program. And the Capitol Police said, you know, if you don't disperse, we were praying in a rotunda. If you don't disperse, we'll have to arrest you. I didn't mind because in a real sense, I'd already been arrested. My mind and imagination arrested by this idea that we as a country abutted in this. And so I was arrested that day, standing up for Medicaid expansion, standing up for healthcare in 2017. My office is now down the hall from that rotunda. I've moved from protest of public policy, from agitated to legislator. And so the work of democracy is an ongoing project. The meaning of a democracy that embraces all of us in our diversity requires a lot of different voices. In a real sense, I talked about the Freedom Caravan that that other needs are led to take Katrina Vackoese back to New Orleans for me. America is a Freedom Caravan. And along the way, we've had to pick up new voices who have contributed to our understanding of what it means to be and Americans. So women have had to stand up for the right to vote. We've had to hear the voices of those who are in the disabilities movement. And we haven't fully recognized the ways in which we've denied them access. Sometimes privileged blinds, African-Americans and other people of color have had to stand up. And it is a country made great, not in spite of our diversity, but because of it. That's what my life's work is about. That's the project that I intend to spend my life working on. You say the project of democracy is ongoing. It's a verb. Absolutely. How is Georgia doing right now? Given Georgia just had primaries, they had pretty high turnout rates. Is it going in the right direction, the franchise in Georgia? Look, as I said, it's ongoing. And I think we've had a primary. a primary is different from a general election, both in terms of the volume of people who will show up. And I think we will see how this plays out. So you are one of the Democrats in the Senate who is up this year. You have to run again for your seat after two years. And the issue on Georgians' minds and American minds is the economy. Inflation is up at historic highs. Gas prices are at $5 a gallon in many, many places. The kitchen table issues are the ones that seem to be driving the concerns of most Georgians and Americans. And your opponents are going to spend millions of dollars trying to tether you to what they call Biden's failed economic agenda. So what is your message? How are you going to make the case that you should be returned to Washington in a year that cyclically is disinclined to be a positive year for Democrats? Well, representing the people of Georgia is a great honor. It's a real honor when the people of your state say we want you to represent us and our children. at the highest levels of American government. And it's a sacred trust that I take seriously. It's the reason why we passed the single largest tax cut from middle and working class families in American history. It's called the expanded child tax credit. I would have liked to see us extended. We passed a bipartisan infrastructure bill. And right now, I'm very much focused on the pressures that ordinary people are feeling in this moment in which we are witnessing global inflation. We saw a pandemic, we're in the throes of it still, unlike anything we've seen in our lifetime, it created economic turn down. And as the economy's opened up, we're seeing these forces at work, coupled with clear price gouging by certain corporate bad actors, which is why I put forward a bill that passed the House, which has made its way to the President's desk. My bill would deal with these international ocean carriers who are clearly engaged in price gouging because they can. As much as a 2000% increase in profits, Georgians are paying. of high prices that to pump oil and gas companies are experiencing record profits. And so I have a bill that deals with that. I've also put forward a bill that would suspend the federal gas tax. Look, certainly until the end of the year, I've also put together another bill that would provide a tax holiday using money that we already passed in the American Rescue Plan. So I don't wake up every morning focused on my concerns. I'm focused on the concerns of the people that I've preached to on Sunday morning, the folks I run into at the grocery store, the seniors that I know who for a very long time have had to decide between buying prescription drugs and buying groceries as big pharma engages in price gouging. I have a bill that would cap the cost of insulin to $35 per person per month. When I do this work, it's not theoretical for me. I'm a pastor. And so I've been with families who have a loved one who has diabetes. I know what happens. I've been there when folks have gotten the news that they've got to get an amputation because the diabetes is out of control or they've got to go on dialysis. $1 out of $4 in our healthcare system is spent on somebody with diabetes. And so when we cap the costs, when we deal with the cost of insulin in a world where people are rationing insulin, I think we go a long way with also addressing some of these inequities in our total healthcare system. Republicans have nominated University of Georgia and NFL legend Herschel Walker to be your opponent in this upcoming November election. Walker was of course, has been endorsed by President Trump and Mitch McConnell. And as I said earlier, millions of dollars are going to go into this Senate race. It is going to be a highly watched and very expensive contest for your seat. Since his retirement from NFL, Herschel Walker has run a company that distributes chicken products and launched companies that have been plagued by deaths and lawsuits. He appeared on the Celebrity Apprentice. He has promoted conspiracy theories about the 2020 election and even cast out on whether President Trump's supporters were truly responsible for January 6th. Is Herschel Walker right for Georgia? Great thing about America is that's not up to me. It's up to the people of Georgia. But I will say that the people of Georgia have a real choice in front of them. And this is going to be a long campaign. But the question is, who's ready to represent the people of Georgia at a very serious time? I've spent my whole life focused on service, focused on trying to make people's lives better. It's not something that I took on as a result of running for the Senate. I was fighting for Medicaid expansion, and then I wrote a Medicaid bill as a legislator. And so I'm deeply honored that I get to do this work for the people of Georgia. And I look forward to having this conversation. Are you saying to Herschel Walker's not ready? I intend to talk to the people of Georgia about their problems and their issues and their hopes and their dreams for their children. And I think that if we stay focused on that, we have a chance to get into public policy, right? Well, you ran an ad earlier in this campaign that really calls out Walker for comments made in 2020 about killing COVID-19 with a dry mist. As you walk through the door, it will cure in it over on your body. When you leave, it will cure the virus. As you leave, it's your product. They don't want to talk about that. Basically, the ads adjust that he's not ready. What are you going to say about Herschel Walker? I'm focused on the work that I'm trying to do. Here's what I'm focused on. You know, I was on a plane coming home during the holidays and there was a young couple in front of me. And they had a baby must have been 18 months old. And they said, we're big supporters of yours. They came up to me after we landed and asked me to sign the back of an airline ticket. And then the mom handed me another ticket that she had. And she'd written a note. She said, we're big supporters of yours. Could you do something about student loan debt? She said that she had borrowed $35,000 trying to get through college. And several years later, she had paid $20,000 on the $35,000, and she still owed $30,000. She said, I feel like I'm in a government-sponsored loan tract. Would you please do something about student debt? You know, I'm the first college graduate in my family. I got through college on Pell Grant's low-interest student loans, and in the years since, things have changed. And student loan debt has now surpassed credit card debt in this country. It has surpassed auto loans. Our children have a mortgage before they have a mortgage. And so I'm focused on them. After all, while I'm in political office, I'm not in love with politics. I'm in love with change. I'm in love with justice and trying to make real this idea that Dr. King always talked about a beloved community, and I'm going to stay focused on that. I can tell you're uncomfortable saying anything negative about your opponent. But how are you going to draw a contrast? Look, I'm going to continue to do the work. The people of Georgia hired me to do a job. and I wake up every morning. You know, it may sound corny, but I still pinch myself most mornings. I can't believe I get to do this work. This is a dream job for somebody like me who has spent my whole life working on criminal justice reform, working on voting rights, working on health care. In this contest in November, you and Herschel Walker will be in a historic contest because either way Georgia is going to send a black man back to the United States Senate. A black Republican, a black Democrat are running against each other to serve the people of Georgia. What does that say about Georgia politics right now? And what does that say about the Georgia Republican Party? We have managed to move the arc of our country in such a way that Georgia did an amazing thing. It sent its first black senator and its first Jewish senator to the United States Senate. And that's significant given the arc of our country's history. And as a result of that, I've been able to pass a bipartisan infrastructure bill. and been able to pass a tax cut the largest for middle-class families and working-class families in American history. And now focused on lowering costs for ordinary families, and I intend to continue to do that work. How will race play into this contest? I think when most folks are sitting around the table every day, they're trying to figure out who's thinking about them. And who's thinking about their problems? You know, I spent a lot of time during my last campaign in rural Georgia. Political pundits like to split us up into these groups, rural and urban. I spent a lot of time in rural Georgia. And I would go into these little towns and folks would be surprised that I was there running for the Senate. I was surprised that they were surprised. because the way I see it, if you intend to be the senator, you intend to be the senator for the whole state all across the state. We've had 10 hospitals to close in the state of Georgia over the last 10 years, in large measure because we've refused to expand Medicaid. When you say Medicaid, when you say hospitals are closing, people might assume you're talking about Atlanta. All 10 of those hospitals are in rural areas. And if you live in a rural area and your hospital closes, it doesn't even matter really that you have income and insurance. If the closest hospital is 90 minutes away and you're having a stroke, you're in trouble. And so here's my thing. I think that more often than not, the right thing to do is also the smart thing to do. It's a kind of enlightened self-interest. I think it's right. to make sure that every citizen has access to healthcare. But I also think it's smart. And if we didn't know that before the COVID-19 pandemic, we ought to know it now, a deadly contagious virus that we were all up against meant that if my neighbor had the virus, she might be sick, but I'm potentially in peril. That doesn't make my neighbor my enemy. regardless of their zip code or their race or by what name they call God who they love. That doesn't make my neighbor my enemy. That means that I am invested in their well-being. And so I ought to want my neighbor to have a mask, a vaccine, whatever we can do. But I should also want my neighbor's children to have access to a good quality education. I should want them to have clean air to breathe and clean water to drink because it's not the king said we're tied in a single garment of destiny caught up in an inescapable network of mutuality, whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly. That's the moral lens through which I look at a whole range of issues from health care to the sustainability of the planet to the future and viability of our democracy. You were very close to the late Congressman John Lewis, a civil rights icon who's funeral. In fact, you presided over at Ebony's or Baptist Church. John Lewis appeared on the original version of Firing Line. What we are trying to do is take some of the ethics, some of the morality, hopefully that existed during early days of the Civil Rights Movement and ejected into the political arena. And how does that translate itself? from what it was that inspired it in the mid 60s to what it is that now approaching the mid 70s you wanted to do. A whole point now I think is to consolidate the games that we have made to build on those games to use the people, use the force, use the energy that we created during the 60s for good. some of the same people, uh, uh, sharecroppers, tenant farmers, housewives and ladies that were very much involved in the city movement, the freedom ride, the whole right to vote. Uh, these people running for office and they're not just going to be another group of elected officials, but they're going to represent a different and a new breed. What would John Lewis say right now about the progress for making in this country? He would tell us to keep moving. You know, he often talked about good trouble. I was his pastor, but he was my mentor. And, you know, I had the honor, as you point out, of presiding over his funeral. And as I was preparing to do that while running for the Senate, I asked myself, what was John Lewis thinking that day when he crossed that Edmund Pettus Bridge? Dressed in a trench coat backpack, he and Joseo Williams Police officers with Billy clubs just on the other side of the bridge. Here's what I know. He was not thinking that one day at the end of his life at his funeral, there would be three American presidents on both sides of the aisle. They are paying tribute to him. He was not thinking that one day he'd be the recipient of a presidential medal of freedom. I think that he was probably just trying to stay alive that day so that he could fight the next day. And yet by some turn and stroke of destiny mingled with human determination. He walked across a bridge and built another bridge to a future that we all now enjoy that allows me to do the work that I'm doing and so many others. And so I think he would tell us to keep the faith and keep working. It's dark, the days are difficult. But who are we to give up? People like him faced improbable odds. I think we look back at moments like the Civil Rights Movement, and we speak as if those gains were inevitable. They were actually quite improbable. They didn't always know what their next steps would be. I've had the benefit of talking to Andy Young and folks like that who live in Atlanta. They didn't know which way to go sometimes, but they kept moving. They kept moving in the direction of progress. We say in the black church, God makes a way out of no way. And that's the title of my book. And I think the unspoken part of that is as we make our way, as we do the work, God makes a way out of no way. Senator, Reverend, Raphael Warnock, thank you so much for being here on Firey Life. Great to be with you.

January 6th featured a violent assault on the U.S. Capitol.
Raphael Warnock is the first Black U.S. Senator from Georgia.
The January 6th Capitol attack was driven by the 'big lie' about election fraud.

A bipartisan framework for gun reform has emerged with support from 10 Republican senators.

Black women in Georgia are three to four times more likely to die in childbirth than white women.

Voting rights legislation previously passed unanimously in the Senate under George W. Bush.

assumptions.text: Democracy depends on active participation and vigilance from citizens, not passive acceptance.
The moral legitimacy of political action stems from spiritual principles rooted in shared human dignity.
Political polarization arises primarily from leaders prioritizing personal power over collective democratic values.
Progressive reforms are achievable through pragmatic collaboration across party lines when grounded in shared public concern.
The historical significance of Georgia’s 2020 elections reflects broader national transformation toward inclusion.
The existence of systemic disparities (e.g., maternal mortality) indicates failures in institutional commitment to equity.
Public opinion generally aligns more closely with progressive policies than current legislative outcomes suggest.
Spiritual conviction provides a valid and necessary foundation for civic leadership and ethical governance.
The integrity of democracy is undermined by dark money, gerrymandering, and disenfranchisement.
Historical movements like the Civil Rights Movement offer enduring moral frameworks applicable to contemporary political challenges.
